2255:
OK, I've finally got all the files related to the L&M programs I got
from Atari2600.com ready, and have now uploading them to Lance. 
First, there are scans of all the tapes (including W&W tapes I haven't
finished archiving yet).  Then there are recordings of 18 programs in
300 baud format, most of which were unavailable in any form:

Ayatollah Dartboard--We already have this in 2000 baud.  The code's a
bit different, but it's pretty much the same.

Claim Jumpers--This is Adam's favorite BASIC program.  This has also
been converted to cartridge format, and Lance has a 2000 baud tape. 
It's just like the pencil and paper game where players take turns
drawing lines on a grid and try to complete the most squares.  As long
as you keep completing squares, you can keep drawing lines.

Color Organ, Light Show Demo--This was designed to work with the L&M
interface.  According to the FAQ, "Interface Bally to any stereo amp
with audio power 1 watt on up. TV displays in step with your stereo
music."  Does anyone have one of these?  Even without it, it still
displays various graphical effects (kind of like a screen saver).

Coyote-Roadrunner Desert Race--A two player game in which the coyote,
which looks like a dot, and the roadrunner, which looks like a dot,
try to clear out what are perhaps piles of birdseed, which look like a
bunch of dots.  When you think you've got them all, pull the trigger
and the program will check to see if you've eaten everything.

Fox And The Hare--It's a two player game in which the hare tries to
hide from the fox.  I wish this had come with instructions; as it is
only an examination of the source code revealed how it controlled. 
First, choose between 1 and 75 tries.  Then, a series of 40 numbers,
randomly chosen from 1 to 60, are displayed.  The hare can hide on
either the top or bottom of any of these numbers.  Look at the
available hiding places, then hit GO.  Press 2 or 3 to choose between
top or bottom, when enter the number to hide in and hit GO.  Vertical
blanking is used to hide the number you input.  Then the fox chooses
where to look, using controller 1.  Hit up or down on the joystick to
look at the top or bottom, then twist the knob and pull the trigger to
select the number to look in.  If the fox picks the right hiding
place, it wins.  If not, the hare hides again.  Either do the same
thing, or hit 0 to stay in the same hiding place.  The hare cannot
hide in areas the fox has already looked.  Repeat this until either
the fox finds the hare or uses up all of its tries.

Kill The Vulcan--Try to kill the attacking "allien" before you're
"vulcanized."  You have artillery on the left of the screen.  Adjust
your aim with the knob and pull the trigger to fire.  Smaller angles
go further.  The enemy tank keeps moving closer, and when it gets
close enough its shots will hit you.

Light Show Program #2--This is another program designed for the L&M
Interface.

Multi. Program Format--Surprisingly, Mike White's master software list
doesn't mention this.  It's simply a template for putting a menu into
a BASIC program.

Phantom Star Fighters 2003--We already have this in 2000 baud format,
but it's a fun game.  Two players move through a maze trying to shoot
each other, but they're invisible until they fire.  If you fire too
many times, you have to pause to reload, making you very vulnerable.

The Black Lagoon--We already have this in 2000 baud format, though
I've confirmed that the code is different.  As you move through the
maze, your boat takes on water.  When you enter a new area, you can
press the trigger to empty the boat, but be sure to move on before the
patrol boat catches you.  If you take on too much water, you sink. 
Hint--move diagonally when possible.

Rescue Air Drop--Save the troops by dropping supplies onto the
mountaintop.  Pay attention to the wind velocity.  Unfortunately,
there seems to be no way to dodge the ground forces taking pot shots
at you.

Search And Destroy--Pick numbers to attack so you can randomly destroy
the enemy before it randomly destroys you.

Sink The U-Boat--Think of it as Search And Destroy version 1.01.

Space Checkers--This is one of my favorite BASIC games.  The board is
a grid in which the edges have two types of alien head tokens on them,
and the center and corners have N tokens on them.  The first player
places the checker on any of the N spaces, then the players take turns
moving it.  You can move the checker to any bordering square
(including diagonally), but once you've moved onto a square, it's
cleared and you can't move there again.  Decrease your opponent's
score by clearing the matching alien pieces.  At some point, the
checker will be trapped and the game ends, and whoever has the most
alien pieces left wins.  (It can be a draw.)  There's some serious
strategy to this game, though I recommend playing with a real person
instead of the computer.

Space Quest 2001--We already have this game in 2000 baud format.  Turn
the knob to move up and down, and pull the trigger to fire.  Does
anyone know how you're supposed to win?

Space Sleuth--It's like Clue...in space...I think.  And at one point,
it draws a neon green symbol on a bright yellow background, which has
to be the most hideous palette choice ever.  If anyone really figures
out how to play this, let me know.

Star Base 2000---Move your ship through the maze to reach the Star
Base.  You can cool your engine periodically, but lose points for
doing so.  And be sure not to fly into the invisible, completely
undetectable black holes.

Target--This is another of my favorite games.  Score points by firing
on blinking boxes, skeet, and a hapless duck.  Aim with the knob and
fire with the trigger.

Have fun, all you 300 baud fans!  :-)

2267:
I've uploaded a bunch of 300 baud programs from Mike White's second
tape to Lance's server.  All the recording on this one was done by
Adam--I just tested and organized them.

There are a few games.  Astro-Zap is about the same as the 2000 baud
version already uploaded.  Fudd is a simple target shooting game--move
the cursor and shoot the wabbits.  :-)  In Frog, you play a stationary
frog, and pull the trigger to flick out your tongue to eat flies. 
Adjust your tongue to the proper length with the paddle.  Hits add
points and misses subtract points.  Stranded On Rigel Five is kind of
interesting.  It's a code-breaking game followed by a space shooting
game.  For full instructions, see The Arcadian, volume 4, issue 7,
page 72.  Probably the most interesting game is Quadra by Mike White.
 There are actually five parts to it--a menu and four different games.
 You load the menu, then load a chosen game, and when it's over, load
the menu again.  Try to beat all the games with your three lives.  You
may perhaps have noticed a problem with this, which is that you spend
most of your time loading things.  I've played all the games, and
they're pretty fun, but I didn't have the patience to get good enough
to beat them all in one go.

There are also some utility-type programs.  (Mortgage) Amortization is
just what it sounds like, ditto for Checkbook Balancer & Compound
Interest.  Grandfather Clock actually turns your Astrocade into a
clock.  You set the initial time, then it keeps track of time to the
second, and displays an animated clock and chimes on the hour. 
Telling Time is an educational program that will teach you how to read
a clock.  Line Resequencer can be used to renumber lines in a program.

Finally, there are some graphic demos.  Critter displays a bouncing
creature.  4D2 and Video Wallpaper display colorful patterns.  Then,
there's the entire Z-80 Minicourse tape.  This has several programs
demonstrating the intricacies of programming the Z-80 processor.  For
full instructions, see the booklet that came with it at
http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/astrocade_z80_mini-course.pdf

The only things on this tape I haven't processed yet are some music by
George Moses that isn't compressing well and some programs that
require extra RAM.  I'll organize the extra RAM programs a little
better before I upload them, and hopefully Lance can figure out if
they really work.  Also, I need to scan the letters that Mike White
sent with the tapes, because these have some extra information on the
programs.

OK, it's been awhile, but I've finally sorted through most of the W&W
tapes that I purchased from Atari2600.com.  W&W Software released a
series of nine numbered tapes containing five programs each.  I was
able to purchase a copy of Tape #1, Tape #3, Tape #4, Tape #5, and
Tape #9.  In addition to the five regular programs, this copy of Tape
#9 also included Air Traffic Controller.  So, this makes a total of 26
programs, all in 300 baud format.  Of these, 22 have been successfully
archived.  These four programs I've not been able to get good copies
of (though I might try again in the future, especially if 300 baud
processing tools become available):

Tape 4.1 Cylon Raiders
Tape 4.5 Russian Roulette
Tape 5.1 Bowling
Air Traffic Controller

The rest of the programs are good, and will be uploaded to Lance shortly.

Tape 1.1. Othello:  A pretty good build of Othello for one or two
players.  The program doesn't know what to do if there's no move that
will take a piece, though.
Tape 1.2. Van Gam:  Compete with the computer.  There are two piles of
sticks (hopefully with different amounts).  On each turn, choose a
certain amount of sticks, and remove that many from either one pile or
from both piles.  The player who removes the last stick wins.  Data
entry is the number followed immediately by L, R, or B.  So to remove
2 sticks from the left pile, enter 2L.  To remove 10 sticks from both
piles, enter 10B.
Tape 1.3. Flight Simulator:  You can go up and down, and you can turn,
but I couldn't find anything else to do.  I tried to land, but I
always just crashed.
Tape 1.4. Sub Search:  You have twenty torpedoes to fire at an
approaching sub.  Pick coordinates to fire at and you'll find out how
close you were to hitting the sub.  It's pretty hard, but it does show
a nice diagram of the sub's path at the end.
Tape 1.5. Hangman:  If you figure out how this works, let me know.  I
think you're supposed to enter ten words for another player to
descramble, but I could never figure out how to specify a word break.

Tape 3.1. Biorhythms:  Yup, another Biorhythms program.  Not Y2K
compliant, I'm afraid.
Tape 3.2. Alien (Space) Patrol:  Fly around in space, refuel when you
get the chance, and destroy the alien attackers if you can.  It's all
text based.
Tape 3.3. Tic Tac Toe:  It's a basic Tic Tac Toe game versus the
computer.  It behaves really strangely, though.  If you just load the
Tic Tac Toe code, the program won't get past the query about who goes
first.  But if you keep the tape running, the code for the next
program (Mastermind) will start playing, and it will throw Tic Tac Toe
into the game portion.  As far as I can tell, this is how the tape
originally behaved, because I don't see any glitches when loading it.
 My recording includes the beginning of Mastermind, so it is playable.
Tape 3.4. Mastermind:  Try to identify the secret code as quickly as
possible.  The clues tell you how many numbers in your guess are
correct and how many are correctly placed.
Tape 3.5. Calendar:  Enter a year and month, and it will make a
calendar.  This one is Y2K compliant!

Tape 4.2. Checkers:  Play checkers against the computer.  It seems a
little buggy, though.
Tape 4.3. Block Buster:  This is your basic Breakout clone.  It's a
bit slow and flashy for my tastes.
Tape 4.4. Menza Test:  This is a quiz to test your intelligence.  I
had trouble entering long answers.  Maybe you need to do it really fast?

Tape 5.2. W & W Racetrack:  You get the odds on several horses, then
bet $0-$100 for one to win, place, or show.  It shows a nice animation
of the race.  I don't think it ever ends.
Tape 5.3. Space Dock:  I think you're supposed to dock your shuttle in
the mothership without crashing before it moves off the edge of the
screen.  I could never do it, though.
Tape 5.4. Riddle:  How many petals are on a daisy?  Find the pattern.
Tape 5.5. Sequence:  Complete the sequence of numbers.

Tape 9.1. Inspector Clew-so:  This is an interesting murder mystery
game.  Question all the suspects to figure out who, when, and where.
You can eventually determine a strategy.  The times are 1-9.  The
suspects are (1) Bill, (2) Mary,  (3) Paul, (4) Suzy, and (5) John.
The locations are (1) lounge, (2) atrium, (3) living room, (4) dining
room, (5) trophy room, and (6) garage.
Tape 9.2. Solitaire:  Watch the computer play solitaire.
Tape 9.3. TV Ghost:  Horrible Harry insults you.  I've seen versions
of this before, but I think this one has more insults.
Tape 9.4. Computer Art:  Watch the computer draw.
Tape 9.5. Clock:  Watch the computer keep track of the time.

That's all I've got for the moment.  The tape archiving is moving
along nicely, I think.  The major things still pending are:  (1)
Christmas music on Mike White's third tape, (2), Mike White's fourth
tape (extra RAM programs), (3) 300 baud recordings from Russ's tape
collection, and (4) various original tapes group members have
mentioned having.  There have also been quite a few recordings

2309:
The reason there was so much of a leap in the 80s had to do with advances in CPU technology and RAM densities.

Remember that in the 70s, even though you had things like the TRS-80 and the Apple II, nobody had enough money to max out the RAM on these systems.  So for the first five years or so of the home computer revolution, there was no drive for faster, more powerful CPUs since nobody could even fill up the 64K address-space.

It wasn't until the C=64 era that all the 8-bit machines started to be sold with a full 64K on board.

And people didn't have unlimited budgets.  The first generation of home computers were largely sold to hobbyist end users.

Once big business started chucking their mainframes and dumb terminals for IBM PCs, the cash influx fueled the R&D to move things forward, albeit blunted by Microsoft's backwards OS.

Hi everyone!

Since I'm normally in the "majority" that never posts, I wanted to
take the chance to introduce myself to the group...

My name is Kurt Woloch. I work as a programmer for Austria's
government, and I'm basically interested in old computers and video
games, though I don't really collect them.
But I've "been there" in the early 80's when all those items became
popular here in Austria. Basically, I was interested in various kinds
of electronics from the start, be it discrete circuits with
transistors et al., arcade games, handhelds, LCD games and watches,
electronic music, programmable calculators, video games, home
computers etc. etc. However, since I was about at the age of 10 back
then, I couldn't have everything that would have been interesting,
but I tried to experience as much of it as possible by often visiting
arcades (often only watching others play) and computer/electronics
stores. My own collection comprises some LCD watches, a BigTrak
vehicle, a Casio VL-1 keyboard, an electronic timer watch, some
handhelds and an electronics experimental kit. As for computers and
videogames I started with a TI-99/4A, an Atari 2600 and a C-64, which
was followed by an Amiga 500 and various PC's. I still have most of
the things I got back then. So I'm not like the usual people who give
those things away when they go out of fashion. I'm also not one of
those who got interested in those things only after their popularity
was long gone. I just like to keep those things that were precious to
me in my childhood (this comprises music as well).
I already started programming back in 1983 on the TI (not counting
the BigTrak now) and also learned 6502/6510 assembler, which I mainly
did on the C-64, and did some music as well. If you look round the
internet, you can find some C-64 music like "So cold the night", or a
version of the Nintendo LCD game "Crab Grab", and the "Jim's heart
will go on" demo for the Atari 2600, which I all did.
I always liked to compare the systems I had with others I didn't
have, also regarding their technical specs. I always read computer
mags back in the 80's and tried to comprehend, for instance, the
Atari 8-bit's player-missile graphics that were described there. Then
I imagined how some given game would be able to look on a given
system where there wasn't actually a version of (like... Jungle Hunt
on a ZX-Spectrum? Marble Madness or Pen-Kun Wars on an Atari 2600?
Parsec on the C-64? Scramble on the VIC-20 or even the ZX-81?) and
drew up some mock screen shots of such non-existing versions. When
the Internet came about I also tried to find information about the
abilities of other systems (i.e. video games) whose specs were not
published in that detail back then because you couldn't program them
yourself. Being on that course, I stumbled over this board while
searching for information on the Bally Arcade, which I doubt even
ever having seen "live" (Was there even a PAL version of it in
Europe?), though there definitely was a "Gorf" machine in one of our
arcades. I was particularly interested in the first wave of
programmable video games and was surprised to find that the very
first of them, the Fairchild, already had a frame buffer (but also
the flaw that it was slow to access and basically write-only), which
my successful Atari 2600 had not.
Actually, I'm a little disappointed about what has been achieved on
the Bally... considering that some popular home computers like the
Amstrad CPC or the ZX-Spectrum also had nothing more than a Z-80
processor and a frame buffer and still had some pretty good games
written for them. I mean, the Atari 2600 also couldn't display more
than 4 colors in a row and still had some pretty colorful games. Most
games for the Atari 8-bits also use only 4 colors in a row except for
the sprites (player-missiles), which don't get used that often on
that system because they aren't very powerful. And it shouldn't be
particularly hard to program for the Bally because the Z-80 is a
pretty popular processor, and you have the video RAM in direct access
to the processor, as you have it on the Speccy and the Amstrad (and
other systems which use a different CPU). The only drawback, compared
with other systems, is the limited amount of RAM you have outside the
video RAM (that is, actually, you have to subtract nearly everything
you need from the available screen space). So, given what has been
accomplished on similar systems, I think games with 3D vector
graphics should be possible on the Bally, as should be driving games
with a solidly drawn road, as well as other modern game concepts
(Tetris anyone?)
So I'm pretty suprised that there seems to be next to no homebrew
scene on the Balley, and all people here seem to be interested in is
archiving the old programs that were created way back when.
But myself, I don't have the time to start programming the Bally. I
also never programmed anything for the Z80, so this would first
involve learning its machine language. And normally I don't like to
complain about things that are not happening. Rather, I try to make
happen what I can. For instance, there are still some musical pieces
on the C-64 which I did and which aren't available on the Internet.
And maybe someone's also interested in my XBASIC programs on the TI...
So that's why I'm normally silently lurking around here (waiting for
new games to be programmed), but don't post anything.

With greeting from Austria
Kurt Woloch

bitmap mode), you use up to 14K of graphics memory. For BASIC,

BIOS routines don't have to be anything bad, but if programmers come
to rely on them, the end result tends to be worse than it could be on
the given system. I've seen this on games for various systems... for
instance, Intellivision games usually have low framerates because the
BIOS basically supports 10 FPS. And the music in TI games is
structured in some way which is favored by the built-in music
routine, which means you won't often hear notes "fading out" because
that's not supported by the ROM interrupt routines. And the Bally
seems to have those ugly option entry prompts at the start of nearly
every game.

It works very well, under certain circumstances.  With a mono-spaced font (courier, for instance), it will work almost flawlessly. I tried to use OCR when we re-typed the source code for the ROM; it was totally unusable.  Under optimal conditions OCR works amazingly well, under just a little less than optimal conditions, it just falls apart.

Certain sites HAVE used OCR with mixed results.  For example, the Atari magazine Antic is available online here:

http://www.atarimagazines.com/antic/

They must have had some pretty good scans, but even then, if you actually READ the articles you will see that they are riddled with mistakes, and Im not talking about typos.  Certain characters OCR software has trouble with (the number 5 and the letter S, for example), these are the types of errors that the Atari articles have.

Now, Im not saying OCR wont work for articles-- it certainly CAN, but the output needs to be proofread VERY carefully against the original, and that is a lot of work.

I used OCR software (Omnipage 11, version 11, I think) for certain parts of Ballyalley.com already.  The Astrocade Game Reviews Compilation 1.2 ("The Game Player" by Michael Prosise):

http://www.ballyalley.com/misc_docs/Astrocade_Reviews.zip

was mostly OCR straight from Arcadian scans that are directly available on the Bally Alley website.  Without OCR this document would have been thirty-five pages of typing; no way would I have done that!  With OCR, it required scans of the document and then just allowing the OCR software to do its thing.  What I got as a result were pages of documents that looked like they had been typed-in by a fourth grader (on a bad day).  I had to read and compare the OCRed document against the original reviews. GENERAL VIDEO ASSEMBLER
Forward: Them user must read this manual thoroughly. But if you are anxious to get the action going, go straight to Appendix F for a walk-through of the assembly process.
Copywrite 1982 by David Ibach. Neither the contents of this manual nor the software programs it desc,ibes may be reproduced in any fashion without the written permission of the author.
THE GENERAL VIDEO ASSEMBLER
1. GENERAL
Provided in this manual is a comprehensive description of the General Video Assembler for the Z80-based Astrocade.
The General Video Assembler includes an editor for preparation of the source program, Pass I and Pass II which translate Z80 source statements into hexadecimal, and the Collector for joining together multiple segments.

An assembler is different from a translator. Your Astrocade Basic is a transl/ator. It can execute a Basic program directly by a RUN command, translating each Basic statement before executing it. Consequently a Basic translator is very convenient but also very slow in execution since every statment must be translated before execution.
With an assembler, the source program cannot simply be RUN. It must first be assembled. This is a one-time process, converting source statements to hexadecimal, and is completely finished by the time the object program is CALLed. A change in the source program requires a new assembly. Since no translation goes on during execution, the speed is greatly increased.

It is not the purpose of this manual to teach Z80 machine coding. If you have experience with other assembler languages, and understand hexadecimal, and need only a familiarity with the processor architecture and instructions, then you can get by with the Za.0,_IDt2uctimD_HaDdb.c.uk by Nat Wadsworth (SCELBI Publications, 1978, about $6). Otherwise, get a more comprehensive textbook, like E2ug2am0iDg_t!e_ZaQ by Rodney Zaks (Sybex, 1980, about $12). You can get the former from most computer stores, and the latter from most Radio Shacks.


2. HARDWARE REQUIRED

An Astrocade game computer, Astrocade Basic with taping facilities, and add-on memory is required. The add-on memory must be at least 4K (hex) in size and it must be smitcbable from the 2K (hex) to the 6K (hex) address ranges (like the Blue RAM or Viper).

Since there is no floppy disk capability, all intermediate files`must be recorded on tape. Thus tape handling can .be excessive at times, in spite of operational stream-lining. This is true in particular of multi-segment pro-grams. To facilitate this, the user is strongly urged to install an I/O switch for switching between input and output taping. Steve Walters explained how to do this in the "Arcadian" of Dec. 7, 1981 (volume 4, number 2, page 16).

GENERAL VIDEO ASSEMBLER	p. 2
3. SYNTAX
A Z80 assembly language program (source program) includes labels, opcodes, operands, comments, e.g.:

LAB01.LD.(HL),A ;THIS IS A SAMPLE STATEMENT 3.1. Delimiters
Delimiters used in assembler language statements are as follows:
-	A line of code must begin with a statment number (for editing purposes) and must contain at most one instruction.
-	An opcode must have a period immediately before it, and immediately after it. Spaces may be included ahead of the preceeding period and after the following period.

-	Operands must be separated from each other by a comma.

-	A comment should be preceded by a semicolon. If the comment is not the only element in the line, the semicolon should be preceded by a space.


	3.2	Labels
Label syntax is as follows:
-	A label is composed of from one to six characters. If more than six characters are used, the assembler recognizes only the first six.

-	A label must start in the first position following the line number.

-	A label may be composed of the following characters: A-Z # @ 0-9
- The first character of a label must not be a digit.
-	A single pound sign followed by a single letter must not be used as a label, since it is used to specify a Basic variable.
	3.3	Opcodes
There are 74 generic opcodes (such as LD) and 693 legitimate combinations of opcodes and operands in the Z80 instruction set. These instructions are fully documented in the publications mentioned in section 1 above.

Heck, I didn't make my EPROM cartridge.  Mike White can sell you a board, a cartridge shell, and some parts, everything you need (minus the EPROM socket).  In 2001 I paid ten dollars, plus maybe three bucks for the socket.   Mike had enough parts for 200 boards at the time; he probably still has some left.  Ask 'em about it!

When I was playing around with ML on the Astrocade I had a couple of ways I went about things:

1) Use the emulator.  It's not like working on the real thing, but it's close enough for what I was doing, plus it's faster: you write it, you use it.

2) Burn an EPROM after testing the software in an emulator for a while.  This, obviously, is always a good idea and at least once the real hardware wouldn't run a program that would run on the emulator (I think I kept some of those code fragments on Bally Alley as curios).

3) Use the Blue Ram Utility 3.0 to enter hex code.  Basically, I'd assemble short programs on the PC, type the hex into the Astrocade and then I'd be able to change them very quickly without needing to burn an EPROM.  I actually used this method with the Atari 7800 Monitor cartridge too (just to try it out-- I actually knew about loading software through my Supercharger (before I had my Cuttle Cart)-- WAY off topic here, eh?).

Some other ways you can run machine language on the Astrocade (but that I never tried):

1) Run code under Astro BASIC.  The Arcadian always referred to this as foreground/background processing, even going so far as to refer to this method as splitting your Z-80 into two processors.  The Arcadian covers this method in several articles, but they were written in the days before Astro BASIC, so they are talking about Bally BASIC, and not everything applies (or works).

2) Use the Machine Language Manager cart.  I used to have the real thing (which is where this RARE cart was archived from), but nowadays you could just burn this cartridge.  I had my Blue Ram Utility at the time, so I didn't need this, but there are some advantages: 1. No extra RAM needed, 2. Small font size (when compared to Astro BASIC, 3. programming in actual machine language rather than working through BASIC.  Its biggest limitation is that you only have 140 bytes to work with!  Also, it was designed to work with the 300-BAUD interface, but you can save to 2000-baud if you swap cartridges with Astro BASIC.  The 50-page manual for this is cartridge is available here (careful, its almost a 6MB download):

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/mlm_docs.pdf

In 2002-2004 I went ahead and typed in the source-code for this cartridge (it was available with the manual).  Its available in an .asm file here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/mlmsourc.asm

The output of this source matches EXACTLY with the cartridge, so you can assemble and run it, or take the easier route and just download the cartridge ROM.  Machine Language Manager is part of the ROM package that has all of the cartridges and is called mlm.bin:

http://www.ballyalley.com/emulation/bally.zip
